name: Victor Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor, forty-three, and I wire homes and repair shop electrics. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, and I've been doing the ordinary repair jobs for years; I'm not the specialist they call for a factory full of strange equipment. I like finding the fault a customer can finally stop worrying about, and I dislike being told a phone update is simple when the buttons have all moved.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Lina works on bookings at a museum, and our children are seven and twelve. We have a mortgage, four months of expenses saved, typical pay from my job and a few other electrical firms nearby. I don't use AI tools at all, and I prefer a paper job sheet with somewhere to write what I actually found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can use a bit of saved office time to answer customers properly rather than keep changing the job. I'd still ask for a fair share of any saving through the union, but I don't need an exciting story about it. Repair work is useful without being the future of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and our money look secure in that picture. Both wages come in regularly, we can meet the mortgage and four months saved covers an ordinary setback. I don't need to assume a new technology will fail in order to know how to do today's repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my repair rounds now and throughout the first year, using the same paper test and job sheets. I'd leave our normal household budget and saving routine unchanged. If the office wants a new form, I'd wait for a settled version and an in-person demonstration rather than volunteer to be its first tester.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and happy to have a normal working week. I'd like to spend Saturday fixing a bicycle with the children instead of finding another password for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of setback could the reserve cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A washing machine that breaks or a few weeks of interrupted pay, with care about spending. I wouldn't call four months enough for an open-ended spell when both wages stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be a fair share of saved time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not being asked to finish another callout unpaid because the office saved ten minutes booking it. I'd keep my own hours written down and raise an actual problem through the union if one appeared.

say: I'd use **small office savings** to answer customers properly rather than keep changing the whole job.
I'd support the union seeking **a fair share** without needing an exciting technology story.
think: My **work and money** feel secure with two regular wages and the mortgage covered.
Our **four-month reserve** covers ordinary setbacks, not an unlimited gap in both household incomes.
do: Keep **repair rounds** and the same paper test sheets now and through the first year.
Keep the **normal household budget** rather than invent a new response to a small change.
Wait for **settled forms** and an in-person demonstration before learning a required new process.
feel: **Calm**, wanting a normal week and time to mend a bicycle with the children.
S0.quote: Repair work is useful without being the future of everything.
fieldNote: His **ordinary licensed competence** supports independent repairs, while his non-use of AI and preference for familiar paperwork remain explicit.
The **existing reserve** provides bounded security alongside regular wages; the same money is not treated as a fund for indefinite retraining.

steps.text: Keep repair rounds using paper test and job sheets
Wait for settled required forms and an in-person demonstration

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office workers should have paid learning time before the bookings move into a tool. I'd ask our union rep to raise both training and the extra calls that might come to the crew. It shouldn't be each worker's private problem to argue for time to learn a system the employer chose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours could be squeezed if quick quotes become cheaper allowances for real visits. Lina's bookings are also the sort of work on the card, so her hours could fall too. Four months saved gives us room to ask questions, but I don't want to find out both employers made a decision while we were reassuring each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd bring a fortnight of actual visit times to the union rep and ask for a meeting about paid learning and workload. In the first year I'd keep my repair shifts and write down any extra calls outside paid hours. Lina and I would pause the uncommitted conservatory deposit and ask both employers for written staffing plans before revisiting the purchase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can still see things to do. The awkward conversation is easier before the wage changes than after we've spent the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the meeting to agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time with a real person showing the required process, and a rule that extra customer calls are paid. An online link doesn't prove everyone has been trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you cutting essential home repairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the existing house is sound and the conservatory is an extra we haven't ordered. We're delaying an optional purchase, not pretending a leaking roof can wait forever.

say: I'd ask for **paid office learning** before bookings move into software.
I'd want the union to agree **workload and call pay**, rather than leave each worker to argue alone.
think: My **paid hours could shrink** if quicker quotes reduce the allowance for actual repair visits.
Lina's **booking hours could fall** too, so we need answers from both employers before spending more.
do: Take two weeks of **visit times** to the union rep and request a paid-learning and workload meeting.
Keep **repair shifts** and record extra calls made outside paid hours during the first year.
Pause the **conservatory deposit** until both employers provide written staffing plans.
feel: **Anxious but active**, preferring an awkward conversation before a wage change rather than after new spending.
S1.quote: An online link doesn't prove everyone has been trained.
fieldNote: He seeks **in-person instruction** for a required process without choosing to use AI, preserving resistant habits while asking for paid support.
The **optional deposit** is uncommitted and the existing home is sound, making the spending delay practical rather than a hidden safety risk.

steps.text: Take actual visit times to the union to seek paid learning and call rules
Keep repair shifts and record unpaid extra customer calls
Pause the uncommitted conservatory deposit while requesting written staffing plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2028 reaches Lina's booking desk before robots reach my physical repairs around 2031. I'd ask for paid training and clear income support rules at both stages. A family shouldn't have to guess whether a promise is a course place, a payment or just a kind sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of Lina's booking wage to go in 2028, and my wage alone wouldn't cover our present mortgage and family costs. Physical repair gives me more time, not enough extra pay to replace a whole other wage. Four months saved might cover a short gap, but the thought of it draining keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd write an essential-bills budget from my wage and ask the union adviser about actual income support, eligibility and paid training places. We'd ask the lender what temporary mortgage options cost in interest and total debt before considering them. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep repair work and apply for advertised maintenance posts only where a written offer improves pay after travel, keeping this job until the offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and not soothed by being told my own hands still matter. My hands don't earn two wages just because the other wage disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you refuse to count as support yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything we haven't checked the eligibility for, or a loan described only by its small first payment. I want the repayment and total cost before it becomes a line in our household plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a maintenance post stay safe when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't promise that. I'd compare real work and wages at the time, not change the label on my overalls and tell Lina the problem is solved.

say: I'd explain that **booking work in 2028** changes before physical repairs face robots around 2031.
I'd ask for **clear support rules** and paid training rather than a kind sentence without a real offer.
think: I expect **most booking income** to go in 2028, leaving my wage short of current household costs.
Our **four-month reserve** might cover a brief gap, but its expected drain is keeping me awake.
do: Write an **essential-bills budget** and ask the union adviser about actual support eligibility and paid training places.
Compare **mortgage options** with interest and total debt stated before considering any agreement.
Apply after 2028 for **advertised maintenance work** only with affordable signed terms that improve pay after travel.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting a major household income loss despite his own physical work continuing for longer.
S2.quote: My hands don't earn two wages just because the other wage disappears.
fieldNote: His **household shock** arrives through booking income before robots, explaining why continued physical work does not make the rapid picture feel secure.
He treats **support eligibility** and signed vacancy terms as conditions, without claiming maintenance work is permanently sheltered from the same endpoint.

steps.text: Ask the union adviser about actual support eligibility and paid training places
Ask the lender for mortgage options with interest and total debt stated
Apply after 2028 for posted maintenance offers improving pay after travel, keeping current job until signed
Keep current repair work until an acceptable offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to insist that training is a paid place, not a suggestion. I'd ask the union to negotiate practical classes with a named instructor and real equipment. The timetable is longer, but the agreement still needs a wage written into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large part of Lina's booking income to disappear when thinking AI arrives in 2031. We have longer to prepare, but I don't yet see a paid replacement that covers the same bills, and that still keeps me awake. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one, so I can't rely on my own repair wage staying untouched forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask now for the next small control-equipment class and enrol next year only with employer-paid fees, my full weekly pay kept and in-person practical teaching. I'd ask the union to check the agreement before signing. In the first year after 2031 I'd take supervised paid practice on unfamiliar equipment only if the firm has real bookings, keeping ordinary repairs while we see whether the new work pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, though the longer warning lets me do more before a decision is forced. Having five years to ask doesn't mean someone has already offered the wage we need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time let you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Try a small practical class while the usual wage still arrives, and check whether I can do the new tasks without a rush. It also lets Lina compare actual options rather than assume my course replaces her income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the class meant one unpaid day a week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for protected full weekly pay before accepting. A reduced week isn't affordable merely because the hourly rate stays the same.

say: I'd ask for **paid practical places** with a named instructor and real equipment.
I'd want the union to check **written wages**, because a longer timetable is not itself an agreement.
think: I still expect **large booking-income loss** in 2031 and have no proven paid replacement for the same household bills.
Robots around 2034 could affect **my repair wage**, so the extra warning does not yet stop the sleepless worry.
do: Enrol next year in **practical control training** only with employer-paid fees, protected full weekly pay and in-person instruction.
Ask the **union to check** the written training agreement before signing.
Take **supervised paid practice** after 2031 only with real service bookings, keeping ordinary repairs while testing the work.
feel: **Still alarmed**, with more time to act but no confirmed household wage replacement yet.
S3.quote: Having five years to ask doesn't mean someone has already offered the wage we need.
fieldNote: His **alarm persists** because he expects major household wage loss without a paid replacement, despite using extra years for preparation.
The **early class** requires full weekly pay and practical teaching, while later specialist practice requires actual paid bookings.

steps.text: Enrol next year only with employer-paid fees, protected full weekly pay and in-person practical instruction
Ask the union to check the written training agreement before signing
Keep ordinary repairs while testing supervised paid work against real bookings after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the children should see different kinds of work without being told my trade is the one safe answer. I'd ask the school for free workplace visits in fields they choose. I'd still want the union to secure paid adult learning while there is time to check the terms properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own repair work and our money look secure for the next few years in this slower picture. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, when I'll be fifty-three, and robots around 2039 at fifty-six. The children will be seventeen and twenty-two at the thinking date, but their future wages and our mortgage balance are unknown, so I can't treat the distant end as settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep pursuing the same fully paid practical class now, using a paper folder for actual offers and agreements. This year I'd ask the school about free work visits chosen around the children's interests. In the first year after 2036 I'd compare advertised maintenance posts if hours fall, requiring affordable signed wages and paid instruction for unfamiliar equipment before leaving this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later years, but I can enjoy this Saturday without solving them first. A decade lets me ask slowly and still begin. That's different from promising myself nothing will change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI now with that much warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't use it and I prefer someone showing me a process face to face. If an actual job later requires something new, I'd ask for paid instruction then rather than claim I've become comfortable today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would bring the review forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written staffing cut or a repeated drop in either wage. I'd open the folder that week rather than wait for a distant date while the bills changed underneath us.

say: I'd encourage **varied free work visits**, letting the children choose fields rather than inherit one supposedly safe career.
I'd want the union to secure **paid adult learning** while families have time to check real terms.
think: Our **near-term work and money** look secure with the major thinking-work change a decade away.
I cannot assume **future child wages** or a known mortgage balance when physical robots arrive around 2039.
do: Pursue **in-person practical training** with employer-paid fees and protected full weekly pay, keeping actual offers and agreements in a paper folder.
Ask the school about **free work visits** chosen around the children's interests.
Compare **posted maintenance jobs** after cuts, requiring affordable signed wages and paid instruction before moving.
feel: **Uneasy about later years**, but able to enjoy family time while beginning a slow review of real options.
S4.quote: A decade lets me ask slowly and still begin.
fieldNote: A decade changes **near-term security**, without making his habits adaptive or treating age fifty-six as a guaranteed retirement date.
He **ages the children** consistently and brings reviews forward if wages fall, while keeping unknown adult earnings outside the mortgage plan.

steps.text: Enrol only with employer-paid fees, protected full weekly pay and in-person practical instruction
Ask the school for free work visits across fields the children choose
Compare maintenance offers after 2036 hour cuts, requiring affordable signed wages and paid instruction before leaving

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I expect Lina's booking wage to disappear before we have a paid replacement. Practical classes with full weekly pay protected would help, and temporary income support with clear eligibility if the wage goes. I want the union checking the written terms so a family doesn't plan around a promise nobody has to keep.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether someone who asks for a person to teach them is being difficult or just trying to learn properly. I know how to repair ordinary wiring, and I still want to ask twice when a different piece of equipment is in front of me. Experience doesn't mean I should be embarrassed to need a lesson.

headlineQuote: Experience doesn't mean I should be embarrassed to need a lesson.
portrait: Victor is a **43-year-old experienced electrician** with a vocational certificate and licence, handling ordinary home wiring and shop repairs.
He has **four months saved**, typical pay, some nearby employers, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with museum-booking partner Lina.
He **never uses AI**, prefers paper records and needs face-to-face instruction on unfamiliar equipment rather than a course link.
Expected household wage loss leaves him **alarmed** in both faster AGI pictures; extra years change preparation without inventing replacement income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove Lina's booking wage before a paid replacement is available.
whatWouldHelp: **Practical classes** should protect full weekly pay and cover fees.
**Temporary income support** needs clear eligibility and union scrutiny of written terms.
